opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that excites me about it is that it moves us from correlational evidence to causal evidence. A lot of interpretability, historically, has been "here's a feature that lights up when the model thinks about deception." That's interesting, but it doesn't tell you the feature is actually *doing* anything in the model's behavior. With ablation, you find the circuit you think is responsible for some behavior, knock it out, and see whether the behavior goes away. If it does, and the rest of the model's capabilities stay intact, you've learned something real about the mechanism.

For safety, that's a much stronger kind of evidence. Say you're worried a model has some capacity for deceptive behavior, or some latent goal that only shows up in rare situations. Behavioral evals only cover the situations you thought to test. If you can identify the internal machinery behind that behavior, you're not limited to the inputs you happened to try. You're looking at the thing that would produce the behavior across all of them.

The other reason I'm hopeful is that the tools have gotten so much better. Sparse autoencoders and dictionary learning gave us a decent vocabulary for what's going on inside these models, and people are now tracing how features connect across layers into actual circuits. A couple of years ago this all felt like it might only work on toy models, and it's been surprising how far it's scaled.

There are real caveats. Models are redundant, so you ablate one pathway and sometimes another one picks up the slack. That's a problem, but it's also informative, because it tells you the behavior is robustly represented. And there's a hard question about whether we're finding *the* circuit or just *a* circuit. But the trajectory is what gets me. If we can get to the point where, before deploying a model, we can say "we found the components responsible for these concerning capabilities, here's what happens when we intervene on them, and here's the evidence they're not hiding elsewhere," that's a much more grounded safety case than "we ran a bunch of prompts and nothing bad happened."

fable-5.1.text:
I think the reason I'm hopeful is that ablation gives you something that most of our other safety tools don't, which is a causal test rather than a correlational one.

Let me unpack that a bit. A lot of what we do when we evaluate a model is behavioral. We prompt it, we look at the outputs, we red-team it, we try to elicit the bad behavior. And that's genuinely useful, but it has this fundamental limitation that you only learn about the inputs you thought to try. The space of possible prompts is effectively infinite, and the model is a very large function over that space. So you're always sampling, and you're always left wondering whether there's some region you didn't sample that behaves very differently.

Interpretability, and circuit-level work in particular, is an attempt to look at the mechanism directly instead of the behavior. And the thing that makes ablation special within interpretability is that it's the verification step. You can have a beautiful story about how a circuit works, you can have attribution graphs, you can have features that light up in suggestive ways, and none of that proves the story is true. Ablation is where you actually intervene. You knock out the component, or you patch in a different activation, and you see whether the behavior changes in the way your story predicts. If it does, you've learned something real about what the model is actually computing. If it doesn't, your story was wrong, and that's also extremely valuable to know.

For safety specifically, I think that matters for a couple of reasons.

The first is about the difference between a model that doesn't do something and a model that can't do something. If I red-team a model and I fail to get it to, say, help with a dangerous bioweapon synthesis, I don't actually know whether the capability is absent or whether I just didn't find the right jailbreak. But if I can identify the circuitry involved in that reasoning, ablate it, and show that the capability degrades specifically and robustly, now I have much stronger evidence about where the capability actually lives and whether my mitigation is touching it. You move from "we couldn't elicit it" to "we removed the thing and here's what broke."

The second reason is around deception and sandbagging, which I think are the scariest failure modes long term. A sufficiently capable model that's trying to look safe during evaluation will, by construction, pass behavioral evaluations. That's the whole point. But it's much harder to fake your internals. The model doesn't get to choose what its activations look like in the same way it gets to choose what tokens it emits. So if you can ask the question mechanistically, "is there a circuit here that's tracking whether it's being evaluated and conditioning behavior on that," and then ablate it and see whether behavior changes, you have a tool that's robust to a class of adversary that behavioral evals are just not robust to.

Now, I want to be honest about why "hopeful" is the right word and not "confident." There are real problems. Ablation has off-target effects. When you zero out a component you can push the model off its natural distribution, and some of what you observe is the model behaving weirdly because it's in a state it was never trained on, not because you removed a meaningful function. Mean ablation and resample ablation help with that, but they don't fully solve it. There's also the problem that circuits in large models are not clean. Things are distributed, there's redundancy, there's superposition, and you can knock out what you think is the mechanism and watch the model route around it. That's a real finding about the model, but it makes clean safety claims much harder.

And then there's the scaling question, which is the one I think about most. The tools work beautifully on toy models and increasingly well on mid-sized ones. Whether we can get them to the point where they give us load-bearing guarantees about frontier models, in the time we have, is genuinely uncertain.

But here's why I land on hopeful anyway. The trajectory has been really good. Three or four years ago we were doing this on tiny transformers and arguing about whether features were even real. Now we're finding interpretable circuits in production-scale models and doing interventions on them. The methods are getting more automated, which is the thing you need for this to scale, because you can't have humans hand-tracing every circuit in a trillion-parameter model. And the field has gotten much more disciplined about using ablation as the arbiter of whether an interpretability claim is true, rather than just publishing pretty pictures.

So I'd say my hope is less "this will definitely work" and more "this is one of the only approaches that even has the right shape to answer the questions we most need answered." Everything else tells you about the surface. This is the one that lets you reach in and test whether the thing underneath is what you think it is. That seems worth betting heavily on.

astra-6.text:
The reason I’m hopeful is that ablation gives you a way to test causal claims about what a model is doing. If you think you’ve identified a circuit involved in deception, you can knock it out and ask: does the deceptive behavior actually disappear? Does the model retain the capabilities it would need to perform the task honestly?

That second question is really important. If your intervention just makes the model less capable, you haven’t learned much. But if you can selectively remove a behavior while leaving other abilities intact, that’s much stronger evidence that you understand something about its mechanism.

You could also turn this around. Suppose a model behaves safely because it has learned to suppress some underlying behavior. Ablating the mechanism that suppresses it might reveal things that ordinary evaluations miss. That would help distinguish a model that lacks a dangerous capability from one that has it but isn’t displaying it.

I wouldn’t treat any of this as a proof of safety. The mechanisms could be distributed or redundant, and your interpretation could be wrong. But it gives us an experimental handle beyond just asking the model questions and judging its answers. You can make a hypothesis about the internals, intervene, and see whether the prediction holds.

r003.rationale: It calls ablation an experimental handle beyond question-based evaluations, but does not compare it with RLHF or claim greater confidence in comprehensively eliminating a behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
The thing that makes me hopeful is that ablation gives you a causal test. If you think you’ve found a circuit responsible for some behavior, you can turn it off and see what changes. That’s a much stronger kind of evidence than looking at an activation and saying, “This seems to correlate with deception.”

For safety, you’d like to distinguish a model that doesn’t have a dangerous capability from one that has the capability but isn’t displaying it during your evaluations. Suppose you could identify and ablate the mechanism that suppresses a particular behavior. If the capability then appears, you’ve learned something that ordinary behavioral testing might have missed.

The hard part is knowing what your intervention actually did. You might just have damaged the model, or the relevant computation might be distributed across several pathways. So I wouldn’t treat a single ablation as a safety certificate. But if you can make specific predictions, intervene, and get the predicted changes while preserving the model’s other abilities, you start to build a much more convincing understanding of what’s going on inside it.
